                    ### Question
                    Question linked to image nº8 A 75-year-old patient with a history of hypertension and hyperuricemia. In treatment with ACE inhibitors and allopurinol 100 mg daily. He went to the emergency room for a picture of several days of evolution of inflammatory rhythm pain in the small joints of the hands of progressive course together with daily fever of up to 37.8ºC. It has raised yellowish lesions on the skin around the interphalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints that in recent days have left a yellowish liquid through the skin. On examination, it presents inflammatory signs at the proximal and distal interphalangeal levels of both hands. A simple x-ray of both hands is performed (see image). Which of the following statements is true in relation to the diagnosis of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. The drainage of yellowish whitish material through the skin is synonymous with infection and requires the initiation of antibiotic treatment immediately.
opb. If the analysis of the synovial fluid showed a cell count between 2000 and 60,000 / μl, it would be a septic polyarthritis and specific treatment should be started immediately.
opc. To establish the diagnosis of tophaceous gout, it is essential that uric acid levels are well above the reference range in all determinations.
opd. To confirm the diagnosis, a complete study of the fluid is recommended.
ope. The diagnostic technique of choice is arthroscopy.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms and history suggest a diagnosis of tophaceous gout. The presence of yellowish lesions with drainage is consistent with tophi, not necessarily infection, so antibiotics are not immediately required. Synovial fluid analysis is crucial for diagnosis; a cell count between 2000 and 60,000/μl indicates inflammatory arthritis, not definitively septic arthritis, thus further analysis is needed. Uric acid levels can fluctuate and are not always elevated in gout, so a diagnosis of tophaceous gout is possible without consistently high uric acid levels. A complete study of the synovial fluid to identify urate crystals is recommended for confirming gout. Arthroscopy is invasive and not the first-line diagnostic method for gout. The retrieved evidence supports the link between hyperuricemia and tophaceous gout, reinforcing the suspicion of gout in this patient.
